sources.title: Ahtna and Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve: An Ethnographic Overview and Assessment
sources.author: William E. Simeone and Odin T. W. Miller
sources.publisher: National Park Service, in collaboration with Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission
sources.annotation: Collaborative ethnographic synthesis using historical records and elders’ accounts. Selected pages document colonial change and forced local displacement; the complete report is not claimed as read. Historical village life is not a template for current institutions.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read acknowledgments and text/captions, printed p.1, pp.112–124 and 130–134 (PDF 13,124–136,142–146); visually verified printed p.131. Other chapters, sensitive site inventory and underlying archival interviews were not independently reviewed.

sources.title: The Ahtna Homeland
sources.author: William E. Simeone, Wilson Justin, Michelle Anderson, and Kathryn Martin
sources.annotation: Community-coauthored specialist study of land relationships and historical dispossession. Distinguishes kin-based rights from imposed property categories. Legal and institutional descriptions remain dated; regional groups, clans, corporations and tribal governments are different categories.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read printed pp.102–103 and 107–116 (PDF 1–2,6–15), including methodological notes; visually checked p.108. Historical rights and settlement accounts were reviewed, not original interviews or current legal status.

sources.title: Inventing the Copper River: Maps and the Colonization of Ahtna Lands
sources.author: William E. Simeone
sources.publisher: Athabasca University Press — chapter 7 in Memory and Landscape: Indigenous Responses to a Changing North, edited by Kenneth L. Pratt and Scott A. Heyes
sources.annotation: Open scholarly chapter comparing changing map purposes and representations. Useful for interpreting mapped absence and continued presence. Its broad continuity language must not erase documented local displacement; historical maps do not determine current ownership.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read selected online analytical text, captions and notes: introduction; Colton 1868, Allen 1887, development maps, Miller 1918 and Ahtna corporate mapping (Figures 7.5–7.9,7.11–7.18). Print pagination and full original archival maps were not independently inspected.

proposedSections.title: Colonial pressures and forced displacement
proposedSections.text: Simeone and Miller’s 2024 assessment combines historical records with elders’ accounts of colonial change. It distinguishes earlier Russian encounters from the expanding American presence after the 1898 gold rush, including mining, roads, schooling and pressures on livelihoods. Its wartime history describes forced removal from Dry Creek in 1942–43: homes were burned or dismantled to make way for an airfield. At Gulkana in 1943, bridge and road construction divided the village and forced resettlement across the river. These were local displacements within a homeland where Ahtna connections continued. The assessment also documents subsequent political organizing. Reading remembered experiences alongside government records matters, especially where official files omit removals. The authors’ synthesis preserves named narrators and differing perspectives; it does not speak for every family.

proposedSections.title: Land, kinship and changing settlement
proposedSections.text: The community-coauthored 2019 study The Ahtna Homeland describes nineteenth-century land relationships through regional bands, matrilineal clans and particular leaders. Winter villages were connected with fishing camps, hunting areas and trails. Rights to use places were recognized, while kinship also carried obligations to share resources, particularly during shortages. This was an organized inhabited landscape before colonial authorities classified land through public and private property. The study follows pressures toward permanent road-connected settlements, including schooling requirements, restricted livelihoods and opportunities for paid work. Its account of movement toward Cantwell shows a gradual process with continued seasonal travel. These historical relationships should be distinguished from today’s tribal governments and Native corporations; none of those categories automatically substitutes for the others.

proposedSections.title: Maps and the visibility of Ahtna presence
proposedSections.text: In his 2022 chapter, Simeone treats maps as historical arguments shaped by their makers’ purposes. He contrasts the sparse Indigenous information on Colton’s 1868 map with later surveys and development maps. A 1918 map used in advocacy over the Copper River fishery instead emphasized Ahtna villages and estimated populations. His discussion also considers a map produced by Ahtna, Incorporated that places corporate landholdings within a larger traditional homeland. Together these examples show why an apparently blank map cannot establish an uninhabited country, and why settlement dots do not capture a whole land relationship. Historical homeland representations, corporate parcels and present legal boundaries answer different questions. The chapter’s interpretations are useful reading guides, rather than authority to draw a precise territorial boundary.

researchGaps: Check original records and additional public family histories for particular displacements; the underlying archival interviews were not independently reviewed.
The 2022 maps chapter gives a 1935 mine-closure date while the 2024 report gives 1938; no mine-closure chronology is adopted here.
Broad homeland continuity does not rule out forced relocation of individual communities.
Current tribal, corporate and heritage-program status requires current community or institutional evidence; historical publications do not verify ownership of linked websites.
Present legal title, ANCSA acreage and regulatory rights require their own authoritative dated sources; the historical synthesis is not a current legal determination.
sourceIndependence: These are three distinct publications, with overlapping authors and underlying records. The 2024 report explicitly parallels Simeone 2018 in places; the 2019 article identifies itself as an expanded version of that book’s introductory chapter. Neither the 2018 book nor separate report chapters are counted here.
limits: No restricted material, site coordinates, detailed burial information or sensitive site inventory reproduced. No main-source edits, publishing or contacts made.
